segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's this theater company in Chicago that, for years, put out a new show every single week where they performed 30 plays in 60 minutes, called the Neo-Futurists. And when we first broadcast today's program all the way back in 2003, a bunch of us were sitting around talking about that group. And one of us had just seen one of their shows. And we thought, that would be really fun-- 30 stories in 60 minutes? Let's try that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Instead of our usual-- each week we choose a theme, bring you three or four stories, blah, blah, blah, public radio, very reflective, what kinds of stories would we end up with if we did 30 in one hour? Or even 20? What would it sound like?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We honestly had no idea. And so, that's what we're going to do today. Today we're going to find out. And I have to say, time is wasting if we're going to fit everything in.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How many will it be? How many will we squeeze in? There is but one way to find out, and that is to stick around.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: And let's begin with this one, Act One-- Don't I Know You? Throughout this hour we're going to be bringing you two-minute documentaries, fantastically short works of fiction, and all kinds of little stories that we ordinarily can't use on the radio show because they are just too short, even though they're really fun stories to listen to and perfect stories for the radio. Our first story is one like that. It's one of those stories-- you know how people you know have their greatest hits stories of things that happened to them? We went on a massive search for stories like that from all over the country, and this is one of the stories like that that we found.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It happened to this actor named Tate Donovan. He told it to our producer Starlee Kine. He was out one night going to a Broadway play with a friend, being treated in this way he never gets treated.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: We're sitting around waiting for it to start. And I'm not a very-- I'm not a sort of a recognizable actor. I'm an actor who works, but I never get recognized.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: So all of a sudden, the 10 minutes we're sitting there for it to start, three or four people come up to me and recognize me. I mean, they know exactly who I am. And they are quoting lines from a television show I was on. And like, hey, you were Joshua on Friends.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And I've always admired stars who were really gracious. So you always think, that's what I want to be like. I want to be really friendly when I'm famous. So I wanted to be friendly and sweet, and go out to the people. They don't have to come to me all the time.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHS] So for a little window of time, though, you were exactly the kind of celebrity that you wanted to always be. You were gracious and reserved.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: Yeah, and warm, you know what I mean? I wasn't like one of these distant celebrities. I was like, hey, I was genuine. They all left thinking, that guy's a really great guy. He's so sweet.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: I was exactly how I wanted to be. I was doing it. I was doing great.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And then the kid with the camera came along. This nervous kid-- I don't know, he must have been 16 years old. He's in a rented tuxedo, unbelievably shy and awkward, and he's got acne. And he's got a camera in his hand.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And underneath the marquee is his date, who is in literally a prom dress, and she's got a corsage. And she's really nervous and sort of clutching her hands. And he sort of comes up to me and he sort of mumbles something about a picture.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And I just feel for him. So I'm like, absolutely, my gosh. Sure, no problem. My God, you poor thing. And I go up to his girlfriend and I wrap my arms around her.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And I'm like, hey, where are you from? Fantastic, you going to see the play? That's great.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And the guy is sort of not taking the photograph very quickly. He's just sort of staring at me. And he's got his camera in his hands and it's down by his chin.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And she's very stiff and awkward. And I don't know what to do, so I just lean across, and I kiss her on the cheek. And I'm like, all right, come on, take the picture. Hurry up.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And finally he sort of snaps it. And I'm like, OK, it was really wonderful to meet you. And he just stammered over to me and was like, um, [CLICKS TONGUE] could you take a picture of us?

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [GROANS]

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: And the whole time, he just wanted me to take a picture of him and his girlfriend underneath the awning of the play. He didn't want a picture of me. He had no idea who I was. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: Oh, God. They were in shock. I don't think they'd ever come across a human being acting this way. I mean, could you imagine-- you ask someone to take a picture, and you just get in it yourself, and kiss them, and hey.

segments.speaker: Tate Donovan
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tate Donovan with Starlee Kine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act Two-- No, Of Course I Know You. One of the things that's been really interesting about putting this show together this week is going to some of our regular contributors and commissioning stories that are just two or three minutes long from people who normally write stories that are 10 times that length. This story is an example of that, from Scott Carrier in Salt Lake City.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: Who was that woman, that woman I just saw while walking out of the restaurant? She was sitting at a table by the door, glasses, a hat, like Lois Lane.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: She looked at me like she knew me. And I said hello because I thought I recognized her. But I couldn't remember her name, so I just kept going out the door.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: Now I can't even remember how I know her. I know I know her, or used to know her. Somehow she was very important to me. She helped me out in a time of trouble.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: She used to roll her eyes. I'd say something dumb and she'd roll her eyes and get me something I needed, even though she didn't have to. Maybe she works in the library, or the county recorder's office, or at the newspaper.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: I think I may have been in love with her. No, she's too young. I was never in love with her, not in that way. It's just that I wanted something, needed something. And she was able to give it to me, almost out of the goodness of her heart. And now I can't even remember who she is.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: I'm sick. I'm old. I should just walk out into traffic and kill myself. At home, at night, I go to sleep, searching for the lost memory.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: Did I meet her down by the river in a canoe, or was it on a ferry in southeastern Alaska, or at the Foreign Correspondents Club in Phnom Penh along the Mekong? She has something to do with water, with life, with mud.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: I sleep poorly, turning and maybe even groaning in anguish. I don't care about the woman anymore. I'm worried for myself. I feel as if there's a black hole in my brain, and slowly but surely, it's swallowing all the memories of my life.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: I get up at 5:30 and drive to work in the dark. I feel terrible. I look like a piece of gum in the gutter.

segments.speaker: Scott Carrier
segments.text: I pull in to Java Joe's to get some chemical help, and there she is behind the drive-up window. I want to tell her I love her, but I don't because it would be too weird. All I can say is, wow. And she rolls her eyes and gets me my cup of coffee.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Scott Carrier in Salt Lake City. If you haven't heard his podcast yet, it's called Home of the Brave.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act Three-- It's Commerce That Brings Us Together. In 1997, Susan Drury and her husband moved to rural Tennessee, not too far from the Alabama line. They grew attached to the local radio station.

segments.speaker: Susan Drury
segments.text: We couldn't really get any other radio stations at the house, but WKSR has a lot going for it-- the way they read the obituaries on the air, the way people call in during the tornado to tell everybody they're OK and where the roads are flooded, the ads from the same downtown stores over and over and over. And then there's the show we like best.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: Here we go. It's time once again for another edition of Swap and Shop here on WKSR.

segments.speaker: Susan Drury
segments.text: Swap and Shop is a low-tech, personable sort of Ebay. It's not fancy or particularly well-produced or anything. It's just a show where people call in to say what they want to sell or buy or give away. They give their phone number, and that's it.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: Swap And Shop, good morning.

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #1: Good morning, I have a couch for sale I need to advertise.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #1: It's a Lane recliner couch. It's six weeks old. It listed for $1,140, and I'll sell it for $600. We've just got one too many.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: OK, and your phone number?

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #1: 468-2524.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: All right, sir, thank you for calling.

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #1: Thank you. Have a good day.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: You too. There's a couch for sale at 468-2524.

segments.speaker: Susan Drury
segments.text: The show is hosted by a guy named Don Estep, and he almost never comments on anything people are trying to buy or sell. He's like a lot of my neighbors, particularly the men. The attitude is, your business is your business. There's no shame in tough times, and nobody turns himself inside out to tell you everything.

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #2: Yes, I have for sale a table and chairs, a microwave, and a washer and a bedroom suite. And I also want to buy a car, a small car.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: OK, there's a table and chairs.

segments.speaker: Susan Drury
segments.text: Mostly you're just left to wonder about the story behind these things. You don't get too many answers.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: Swap and Shop, good morning.

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #3: Yes, I'd like to buy a used trampoline. It doesn't matter what shape it's in or if it even has a tarp on it or not. And my telephone number is 629--

segments.speaker: Susan Drury
segments.text: Swap and Shop is not unique to this station. Local stations across the country have these radio classifieds type shows. WKSR's version has a regular segment called "The Doggone Show."

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: Folks have found a black, white, and brown young female beagle with a white tip on its tail, and, more than likely, a family pet. If you'll call 565-4505-- is that number. Also four cows have been found. And you think they might belong to you--

segments.speaker: Susan Drury
segments.text: That first winter in our house, we had no heat, which we thought was adventurous, but was, in fact, just cold. And when we heard a lady call in with an ugly but functional wood stove for sale for $75, we called her. We got it, and we were toasty.

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #4: Hey, Don, that little black and brown and white beagle with the tip on her tail that we found? Well, we lost her, so you can quit advertising-- on Barnett Road.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: On the Barnett Road?

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #4: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: Radio Caller
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RADIO CALLER #4: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Don Estep
segments.text: Thank you for calling.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Susan Drury, Tennessee.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act Four-- The Sound of One Hand Waving. For this one, let's go to the beach for a one-minute and four-second vacation on Nantucket Island.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [WAVES CRASHING]

segments.speaker: Patty Martin
segments.text: When we were in the water and we realized we weren't able to get back in, we had some friends that were on the beach. And so we started waving to them. We were kind of doing this double-hand wave thing over our heads.

segments.speaker: Patty Martin
segments.text: And our friend just kept waving back. She was standing and talking to some other people on the beach. That must have happened two or three times. And we waved like crazy, and she waved back.

segments.speaker: Patty Martin
segments.text: And then when we got on the surfboard later, when the surfer picked us up and we still couldn't get in, we were waving again. And again she thought-- we asked her afterwards, why did you think we were waving? She said, we thought you were just trying to show us you were on the surfboard with this guy.

segments.speaker: Patty Martin
segments.text: So I'm like, God, we're waving frantically to tell you what, that we're on a surfboard with some 19-year-old, and we're-- Nobody got it. And we were sufficiently panicked. And nobody saw anything but a bunch of middle-aged women at Fat Ladies Beach, waving to their friends.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Patty Martin from Nantucket. She talked to Jim Sulzer. She has since passed away.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act Five-- The Sound of No Hands Clapping. This one came from Vicki Merrick and Eric Kipp and Jay Allison, who's the voice you hear.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Listen.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: [WET SUCTION CLAPS]

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Scallops clapping on Martha's Vineyard.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act Six-- Reaching Out With Radio. Blunt Youth Radio is this project where they work with incarcerated teenagers. This story comes from Long Creek Youth Development Center in South Portland, Maine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And just imagine how this works-- you're a teenager. You're locked up. You're in juvenile detention. And this group comes to you and says they will help you make your own radio story on a subject that concerns you. What do you do that story about? Well, here's Joey.

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: Hi, I'm Joey, and I ate somebody's urine. It all started when I went to dinner at the cafeteria and someone told my friend not to eat the pudding. Then my friend told me, after I ate, that someone had peed in it. I survived that day, but I couldn't stop thinking about it. So I went to the cooks to see if they had an answer.

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: This is Joey and Jake. We're about to see if we can interview Bill Wyman on--

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Our food situation.

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: --people messing with our food.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Yeah, we're not too happy.

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: We're not too happy. Excuse me, Mr. Wyman? I was wondering if I could interview you and talk to you about people putting-- if it happened-- glass in our pancakes and peeing in the pudding and stuff? We was wondering what you had to say about that.

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: They don't. Nobody does that. You kids don't handle the food at all.

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: We heard that it was brought up at briefing that somebody put glass in the pancakes.

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: No, that wasn't glass. It was a piece of plastic that came from one of the glasses out there in the dining room that you kids had.

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: Do you know how it got into the pancake batter?

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: It didn't get into the pancake batter. It was put in there afterwards.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Well, we heard different from other kids.

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: You hear different? Do you know anything about it?

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: We heard that it was--

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: Did you two have any idea, whatsoever, what's going on?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: That's why we came to you, to get an idea.

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: No, that's not why you came to me. You came to me because you thought it was true.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Yeah, of course. If--

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: Then you kept it going.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: If somebody said that they messed with your food, joking or not, wouldn't you want to know really what happened or not?

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: No, I would totally go with the kitchen, with the kitchen crew, and what you guys have been told.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: So you'd believe the kitchen crew over the person? No matter how much credibility you can give them, you'd believe the kitchen crew over them? Even if--

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: Of course, because you don't cook the food. You think it's funny, don't you? You really think it's funny.

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: No, I really don't think it's funny.

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: Then why are you grinning like a Cheshire cat?

segments.speaker: Jake
segments.text: Because you're going friggin' zero to 10 just because we're asking a bunch of questions.

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: No, it's what you're asking. It's how you're asking the same thing over again. And you're trying to get an answer, which there isn't any answer there.

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: All right, this is obviously not working. I'm going to have to interview somebody else. I heard some kid got jumped because he supposedly peed in the pudding.

segments.speaker: Bill Wyman
segments.text: Supposedly. That's the key word right there-- supposedly.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: We have an investigator, and he investigated the incident. And we also had the pudding tested. They took it to an independent laboratory and tested it, and it was proven that there was no foreign matter in that pudding at all.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Now, perhaps you weren't told that because I don't think you're told everything. But it was sad that, because you thought there was, you incited a riot in the dining room and made a big mess that kids had to clean up that had nothing to do with it.

segments.speaker: Joey
segments.text: I don't know what to think. If someone did contaminate the food with bodily fluids, I guess I'd rather not know since I'm stuck here and I have to eat the food. Thank you for your time. This is Joey.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Joey-- he was 18 when he recorded that story. His friend Jake was 16.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: If you're just tuning in, this is This American Life. We have tossed out our regular way of doing the show this week-- trashed it, chucked it, spurned it. We laugh at it, we spit on its grave. And instead, we are bringing you as many short stories as we can fit into 60 minutes. It is barely, what, 18 minutes into the show, and already we are at Act Seven, an incredible achievement.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act Seven-- Up Where the Air is Clear. We have this story from Jonathan Goldstein.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Before he ever moved to Gotham City, before he grew into the overweight, obsessive sad sack of his later years, the Penguin was a poet and a dandy who lived in London. He wrote complex villanelles and threw lavish dinner parties at which he only became more charming the more he drank. He wore a monocle, a top hat, and carried an umbrella.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: One evening, at one of his dinner parties, after hours spent sipping absinthe, the Penguin ran up to the roof of his building, opened up his large black umbrella, and leaped off into the air. As he coasted to the ground, he hollered out lines from Blake, stuff about grabbing life by the fat of its stomach and giving it a twist. He was that crazy. He was that bursting with life.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: From that night on, he made it his habit to jump off roofs ever higher, while clutching an umbrella. After a while, he got pretty good at it, too. He saw that by kicking his legs and twisting his back a certain way, he could actually prolong his flight, coasting all over the place, sometimes only landing after several daring minutes aloft.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It came to pass that the Penguin started hearing more and more about a certain nanny named Mary Poppins. She too, he was told, had been floating around London hanging from an umbrella handle. Everywhere he went, the Penguin kept hearing about her, how it was simply insane that they had not met each other yet.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: So finally, a dinner party was arranged by someone who knew them both. And on the evening of the party, the Penguin walked into the drawing room, saw Mary Poppins on the divan, doffed his top hat, and bowed low, as was his style in those days. He'd planned a few things to say and do when first meeting Mary Poppins. He thought he might lift up his umbrella as though challenging her to a duel. He imagined she would smile and take up her own frilly, perhaps pink, umbrella, and then together, they would dance about the room, leaping over furniture, parrying and thrusting, perhaps even winding things up, breathing heavily nose to nose.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Instead what happened was the Penguin became very shy and quiet. As he stood there staring at her, his top hat felt needlessly clumsy, his monocle too small for his face. And the squinting needed to keep it in place was giving him a slight headache. For the first time in his life, the Penguin felt ludicrous.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I imagine you two must have an infinite amount of things to speak of, said their host as he sat them together at the dinner table. The Penguin nodded uncertainly. After three or four minutes, it became clear that the Penguin and Mary Poppins had absolutely nothing to say to one another that did not deal exclusively with umbrella travel-- getting stuck in trees, the shoulder aches, anxiety about tipping over in the wind.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Everyone at the table just sat there, staring at them expectantly, which made the whole thing even more awkward. Trying to move things along, Mary Poppins asked the Penguin if he liked to sing, to which the Penguin responded, only when I'm drunk. Then she asked if he enjoyed children, to which he replied, yes, in a sweet wine sauce.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: The Penguin then asked Mary Poppins how she kept people from looking up her skirt when she flew. She smiled politely, then turned to the man on her left and asked him how he was enjoying the lamb. The man on her left was wearing an elegant, aristocratic cape. Mary, a bit drunk on the sherry, noted that if he spread his cape out, he might be able to glide about like a bat. The man on her left chuckled and suggested that, after dinner, they head up to the roof and give it a try, which they did.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jonathan Goldstein-- he's the host of the podcast Heavyweight, which feels exactly like this story except the people in it are not fictional.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act Eight-- the Greatest Dog Name in The World. Yes, we have the true story of its origin. Years ago, an exclusive told by two brothers, one of whom is 12, the other is 13.

segments.speaker: Valion Lotze
segments.text: I wanted to name him Pasta. I used to like pasta a lot. And it was probably the first thing that came to my mind, so out of nowhere, I said Pasta. So he said Batman.

segments.speaker: Paris Lotze
segments.text: I wanted to name him Batman because I saw, in a movie, the dog stuck his head out the window and his ears went straight up. And it looked like-- it reminded me of Batman.

segments.speaker: Valion Lotze
segments.text: And we fought over it for a little bit.

segments.speaker: Paris Lotze
segments.text: I just remember running around and chasing each other. I was jumping on my mom's bed, saying, Batman, Batman, Batman. And then my brother was sitting in the chair, saying, Pasta, Pasta, Pasta. And that must have gone on for an hour.

segments.speaker: Valion Lotze
segments.text: I think it was right around the time we had this big fight about gumballs, which I'm not going to get into because it was pretty embarrassing. But if there was just some little thing that we couldn't agree on, then it would just blew up into this whole big thing.

segments.speaker: Paris Lotze
segments.text: Yeah, I remember being pretty upset about it. And then my mom comes in and says, all right, that's it. It's over. It's Pasta Batman. That's it.

segments.speaker: Valion Lotze
segments.text: And then there was silence. And then from there, he was Pasta Batman Lotze. Pasta. [CLAPS] Come on, Pasta Batman.

segments.speaker: Paris Lotze
segments.text: Pasta, here. Pasta Batman. Hey, good doggie.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Their names? Valion and Paris Lotze, age 12 and 13. They spoke with Katia Dunn.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act Nine-- Of Dogs and Men. Elaine Boehm used to work at a pet shop.

segments.speaker: Elaine Boehm
segments.text: We've had to help people select items for their animals. And this woman and her husband came in. She was looking for a training collar, the pinch collar type. And, of course, they're pretty hideous looking, but they do do the job. And they don't hurt the animal, they just get the animal's attention.

segments.speaker: Elaine Boehm
segments.text: Well, she couldn't make up her mind what size to get. So she looked over to her husband and she said, dear, come over here. And then she looked at me and she said, his neck is about the same size as the dog. Put this on, she says.

segments.speaker: Elaine Boehm
segments.text: And the guy stood there and took it as she puts the prong pinch collar around his neck. And she gives him a yank.

segments.speaker: Elaine Boehm
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Elaine Boehm
segments.text: And he says, yes, sweetheart, this works. This works. Thank you very much. That was the end of that.

segments.speaker: Elaine Boehm
segments.text: [BIRDS CHIRPING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Elaine Boehm talked with Jim Sulzer.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act 10-- so let's close out this part of our show before the break with a story from the theater group that gave us the idea for today's jam-packed little program in the first place-- that group, again, the Neo-Futurists. Every single week for over two decades, they did these shows where they would perform 30 plays in 60 minutes. Turns out you can get across a surprising amount in a two-minute play.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Some of their plays are monologues, some of them are scenes. But a lot of them just take some simple concept, one idea, and then spin that concept out on stage for two minutes. This one's like that.

segments.speaker: Greg Allen

segments.text: Coming up, David Sedaris on an important-- and I have to say-- undiscussed question about cell phone use, and so many, so many other little stories, I don't even want to count them, in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Well, this is turning out to be an interesting show, isn't it? It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. And if you're just tuning in, this week we are throwing out our regular way of doing things-- you know, three or four stories on some theme, blah, blah, blah. To hell with all that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Instead, we are trying to cram as many stories into one hour as we humanly can. We guarantee 20. There may be more. We are at number 11, Etiquette Lesson. Here's writer David Sedaris.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: In a men's room at LaGuardia Airport, I watched a man take his cell phone from his jacket pocket, step into an empty stall, and proceed to dial. I thought he had come for the relative privacy, but looking through the space beneath the door, I saw that his pants were gathered about his ankles. He was sitting on the toilet.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: Most airport calls began with geography. I'm in Kansas City, people say. I'm in Houston. I'm at Kennedy. When asked where he was, the man on the phone said simply, I'm at the airport. What do you think?

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: The sounds of a public toilet are not the sounds you would generally associate with an airport, and so his 'what do you think' struck me as unfair. The person he was talking to obviously felt the same way. What do you mean what airport, the man said. I'm at LaGuardia. Now put me through to Marty.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: A few hours later, I was in Boston relating the story to my sister, Tiffany. I mean, he actually placed a call while sitting on the toilet. Tiffany is big on rules, and so I expected a certain degree of outrage. I wanted disgust, but instead, she said only, I don't believe in cell phones. But you do believe in talking on the phone while sitting on the toilet?

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: Well, it's not a belief, she said, but I mean, sure. When asked how she explains the noise, Tiffany scrunched up her face and held an imaginary receiver to her mouth. I say, (STRAINING) don't mind me, I'm just trying to get the lid off this jar.

segments.speaker: David Sedaris
segments.text: Her face returned to normal and I thought of all the times I had fallen for that line, all the times I had pictured my sister standing helpless in her kitchen. Try tapping the lid against the countertop, I'd said, or rinse it in hot water, that sometimes works. Eventually, after much struggle, she would let out a breath. There we go, she'd say. I've got it now. And then she would say thank you. And I'd hang up thinking, well, it's a good thing she called me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Sedaris. His new book Calypso comes out this May.

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: Girls babysit a lot and boys don't. And girls understand that, when you babysit, part of the deal is that you get to eat anything you want. So after we'd put the kids to bed, I said, well, we should go see what they have to eat.

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: And he said, we can't eat their food. And I said, of course we can eat their food. What do you mean? And he said, that's stealing.

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: I said, John, I promise you, it's fine to eat something. They expect us to. They understand that-- they don't expect us to starve while we're babysitting.

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: And finally, he said, well, we can eat something, but only something they won't miss. And they had a huge crate full of grapefruits, and they also had cans and cans of black beans.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: [LAUGHS] So I had half a grapefruit. And John opened up a can of black beans and had that. And then I wrapped up the other half of the grapefruit. And John cleaned-- well, rinsed out and dried off the empty can of black beans. And we put the wrapped-up half a grapefruit and the cleaned out can of black beans in his bag.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHING] So that people wouldn't know that you had eaten anything?

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: We had destroyed the evidence. And this--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At his insistence?

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: Yes, it was absurd. And then we watched TV, our hunger satisfied. And then the couple came home, and we made small talk.

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: And then John picked up his bag in the hallway and there was a sort of dull thud, and half the grapefruit fell out on the floor. And I said, oh, that's mine. I'm sorry, I-- uh, we're allowed to take a piece of fruit from the dining hall. And I had taken that grapefruit from the dining hall, and that's why I have it here.

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: And then they sort of said, oh, OK, OK, that's nice. And then I put it back in John's bag. And then John picked up his bag again, and there was-- you guessed it-- a clang. And clanging out onto the floor went this empty can of black beans.

segments.speaker: Catherine
segments.text: And when the can fell out on the floor, John said, oh, that's mine. I keep change in that. Like, I keep change-- [LAUGHS] as if that was less insane.

segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act 14-- Call in Colonel Mustard For Questioning, Or That's What Happens If You Don't Use a Condiment, Kids. See all the stupid jokes that you end up telling if you have a story that takes place in a hot dog factory about hot dogs? Here we go.

segments.speaker: Jim Bodman
segments.text: My name is Jim Bodman and I'm the chairman of the Vienna Sausage Company in Chicago. And the building that we are currently standing in, which is on the north side of Chicago, on Damen near the corner of Fullerton, was built around 1970.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This hot dog plant, Jim Bodman says, replaced the company's original facility.

segments.speaker: Jim Bodman
segments.text: So it was put together in a Rube Goldberg kind of arrangement. So we moved into this building. And this was a brand new, state of the art, stainless steel, refrigeration is perfect, spit clean building. And we started making our natural, old-world hickory smoked, natural-casing hot dogs here. And it wasn't as good.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They tasted OK, he says, but they didn't have the right snap when you bit into them. And even worse, the color was wrong. The hot dogs were all pink instead of bright red. So they tried to figure out what was wrong.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The ingredients were all the same, the spices were all the same, the process was all the same. Maybe it was the temperature in the smokehouse. Maybe the water on the north side of Chicago wasn't the same as the water on the South side.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They searched. They searched for a year and a half. Nothing checked out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then one night, a bunch of guys from the plant are out having a drink, gabbing about the good old days, back in the old plant on Maxwell Street. They start talking about this guy named Irving, one of those guys who knows everybody in the plant, has nicknames for everybody. And listen to what Irving's job was. Every day, he would weave his way with the uncooked sausages through the maze of passageways in the old plant.

segments.speaker: Jim Bodman
segments.text: He would go through the hanging vents. That's where we hang the pastrami pieces, and it's quite warm. And he would go through the boiler room, where we produced all the energy for the plant. He would go next to the tanks where we cook the corned beef, finally get around the corner, and in some cases, actually go up an elevator. And then he would be at the smokehouse. He would put it in the smokehouse and he would cook it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And as they were telling stories about Irving-- Irving this, Irving that-- a light bulb goes off. In the fancy new modern plant, there was no Irving. Irving didn't want to commute to the north side.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There was no maze of hallways. There was no half-hour trip where the sausage would get warm before they would cook it. In the new plant, they just stuffed the sausages in a cold room and cooked them in a smokehouse in the room next door to it. Irving's trip was the secret ingredient that made the dogs red. So secret, even the guys who ran the plant didn't know about it.

segments.speaker: Jim Bodman
segments.text: So we said, oh, my God, that is, of course, the reason. Why didn't we know that? That's the dumbest thing in the world to not realize. It's right there.

segments.speaker: Jim Bodman
segments.text: How do we fix it? And the solution to the problem was the room that we're standing in right now. And this was a new addition put onto the plant about two years after we built the facility.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So you had to build this room?

segments.speaker: Jim Bodman
segments.text: This whole room-- the outside bearing wall is that wall right there. We put this whole room on. And in this room, we emulate the old area of the old plant.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so this room, essentially, is to simulate Irving?

segments.speaker: Jim Bodman
segments.text: That's exactly right. We should have called it Irving-- Irving's Corner.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's warm in Irving's corner, and it smells nice, too-- smoky, like hickory smoke and spices. Since I first heard this story years ago on a tour of this very plant, I found myself telling it now and then. I think that what I love about it is the fact that these guys at the factory had done everything right-- finally built their dream factory with the best equipment and expertise that money could buy. But you can't think of everything. Sometimes you have no idea why you were a success in the first place.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act 15-- Mr. Prediction. In the mid-1980s, right out of college, David Rakoff moved to Japan and pretty soon ended up in this office job where he was convinced that he understood a secret about the company and its business that nobody else, not even the big bosses at the company, could see. It was like that from the start.

segments.speaker: David Rakoff
segments.text: Primarily, the office was an advertising agency. But what they were setting up was this thing for expatriates who were living in Tokyo at the time, or perhaps all of Japan. And it was like a network on a computer. And they would set up a newsletter on the network, and people could quote, "log on" to the computer and talk to one another, or do research.

segments.speaker: David Rakoff
segments.text: And I was just-- I don't know, I just looked around the room and I saw these computers and could only think, what kind of loser would log on to a computer, talk to someone? Then, in fact, that night in my diary, I had written something like, this is like those comic book enthusiasts who actually read the little instructions at the bottom of the panel that said, for more on the Green Goblin, check out Spidey #137, from the editor.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: David Rakoff
segments.text: And in almost the only moment of decisiveness in my entire adult life-- I've certainly never equaled this-- I went in the next morning and I quit. And all I could think was, sayonara, suckers. Good luck with your network. And we know exactly what the network was. It was the internet.

segments.speaker: David Rakoff
segments.text: I have a negative capacity to identify trends. Like, when in college, I went to see Madonna at Danceteria, which was a club downtown, in like 1982 or whatever. And I thought, boy, is she lousy.

segments.text: Are there other examples besides Madonna and the internet?

segments.speaker: David Rakoff
segments.text: Other than Madonna and the internet, you need another example? When I was an editorial assistant working in publishing, I was handed a manuscript to read. I think I wrote something like, sub-literate, borderline misogyny, an easy pass.

segments.speaker: David Rakoff
segments.text: And somebody thought, I'm just going to take a look at this anyway. It was Men Are From Mars, Women Are From Venus.

segments.text: These are not like me saying, I don't think Alicia Silverstone is going to be very good in Clueless. I mean, these are like--

segments.text: Pretty big, iconic ones.

segments.speaker: David Rakoff
segments.text: Yeah. It was like, have you fellows heard that crazy lunatic in the market place inveighing against the Pharisees? He'll burn off like so much morning fog. We'll never hear about him ever again. It's just like that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Rakoff-- the final book that he wrote before he died in 2012 is a book I just love. It's a novel in rhymed couplets-- Love, Dishonor, Marry, Die, Cherish, Perish: A Novel by David Rakoff.

segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: You're listening to This American Life, where today, it is all about speed. We are, what, 43 minutes into the program and we have already finished 15 acts? And this brings us to Act 16-- That One Guy at the Office. So if you work at a big office, you know that there's always at least one person whose name you do not know. In Jordana's office, Matt is that guy for, perhaps, as best as anybody can figure, half the people who work there. Jordana will tell you about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [PRINTER PRINTING]

segments.speaker: Jordana Gustafson
segments.text: Matt Ostrower sits next to the printer in the busiest hallway at our office. People walk by him dozens of times a week on their way to retrieve printouts. And though he actually works in the New Media department and has nothing to do with the printer, most people don't know this. It's his sad fate that most of his conversations at work are about one thing.

segments.speaker: Matt Ostrower
segments.text: Originally a lot of them were printer-based-- why is this printer taking so long? Oh, the paper's out. Oh, this printer jammed. Some of it's never really left that genre of conversation. They don't really spend too much-- so a lot of it's just very superficial.

segments.speaker: Employee
segments.text: Hey, did you just throw away any printouts here?

segments.speaker: Matt Ostrower
segments.text: No, no, I didn't touch anything.

segments.speaker: Jordana Gustafson
segments.text: I'd been working in the office a few months when, one day, a friend called me and said he was hanging out with one of my coworkers who lives in his building. Who, I asked? Matt, he said. I had no idea who that was and said so.

segments.speaker: Jordana Gustafson
segments.text: Then I heard a voice in the background say, tell her I sit next to the printer. And that's when his predicament hit me. So I decided to survey my coworkers to see if they knew who he is, what his real job is. Do they even know his name?

segments.speaker: Employee
segments.text: No, I mean, I know his face very well. I stop, I chat. I say, 'hi, how are you' as I'm grabbing things off the printer.

segments.speaker: Employee
segments.text: I ask him about his little electronic music devices and all that, and we chitchat. And I'd say I do that probably about three or four times a day at least. But I have no idea what his name is.

segments.speaker: Jordana Gustafson
segments.text: I wondered if Matt was at all surprised by this.

segments.speaker: Matt Ostrower
segments.text: Shocked. I honestly see him between 50 and 75 times a day-- different intervals of time-- at least that, every day. Every single day.

segments.text: And Matt's response?

segments.speaker: Matt Ostrower
segments.text: I'm a little surprised because I see her every day as well.

segments.speaker: Jordana Gustafson
segments.text: I'm wondering if you know the name of the guy that sits in the hallway next to the printer.

segments.text: I don't see anybody sitting in the hallway next to the printer. I didn't think we had anybody sitting next to the printer.

The whole situation is just ridiculous-- that I've been here for a year and a half, pretty much every day, and there's still people who don't know my name or what I do. And it's a little bit weird. I could go through a pretty full day without talking to anyone besides the requests from the printer. Sometimes that's it for me. [CHUCKLES]

segments.text: Matt says the printer shows up in his dreams sometimes. In his dreams, he'll be at a party waiting in line for the bathroom, or at a parking lot at the beach, people everywhere. And there will be the printer, off to the side, chugging away, occasionally jamming.

segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act 18-- Party Talk. Here's writer Chuck Klosterman.

segments.speaker: Chuck Klosterman
segments.text: This was a conversation that happened to me at a party two years ago. At one point in the conversation, I suddenly found it necessary to mention that Journey was rock's version of the TV show Dynasty. This prompted a spirited debate we then dubbed, "Monkees Equals Monkees."

segments.speaker: Chuck Klosterman
segments.text: The goal of this game is to figure out which television show is the closest philosophical analogy to a specific rock and roll band. And the criteria are mind-blowingly complex. It's a combination of longevity, era, critical acclaim, commercial success, and, most importantly, the aesthetic soul of each artistic entity.

segments.speaker: Chuck Klosterman
segments.text: For example, the Rolling Stones are Gunsmoke. The Strokes-- Kiefer Sutherland's 24. Jimi Hendrix was The Twilight Zone. Devo was Fernwood 2Night.

segments.speaker: Chuck Klosterman
segments.text: Lynyrd Skynyrd was The Beverly Hillbillies, which makes Molly Hatchet Petticoat Junction. The Black Crowes are That 70s Show. Hall and Oates were Bosom Buddies.

segments.speaker: Chuck Klosterman
segments.text: U2 is M.A.S.H. because both kind of got preachy at the end. Dokken was Jason Bateman's short lived sitcom, It's Your Move. The Eurythmics were Mork and Mindy.

segments.speaker: Chuck Klosterman
segments.text: We even deduced comparisons for solo projects, which can only be made to series that were spawned as spin-offs. The four Beatles, post-1970, are as follows: John equals Maude, Paul equals Frasier, George equals The Jeffersons, and Ringo equals Flow. David Lee Roth's solo period after Van Halen was Knot's Landing. So there's proof-- marijuana makes you smarter.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Chuck Klosterman reading from his book called Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs: A Low Culture Manifesto.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act 19-- The Hard Life at the Top. Here's a ritual that takes place every summer on the last day of June-- 1,200 new army cadets, mostly teenagers, survivors of one of the most exhausting application processes in the country, arrive at West Point. And then, in the space of one morning, they're separated from their parents. Their clothes are taken away. Their hair is taken away.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They're weighed. They're measured. They're issued a bag, an army uniform, and underwear. They take their oath of office.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then, here is the first act they have as non-civilians. All they have to do is say a single sentence. Once they get it said, they can go to their barracks, but not until then. David Lipsky spent four years writing about these guys and describes what happens each year.

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: The drill is simple. The new cadets have to step up to a tape line, drop their bags, and make their report to upperclassman wearing red sashes. You will walk up to the line, the red sashes tell them. And you will say, sir, new cadet Doe reports to the cadet and the red sash for the first time as ordered.

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: The new cadets swallow, nod their heads, and then the screwing up begins. This cadet is so nervous, he doesn't realize he's supposed to swap his own name for Doe.

segments.speaker: Cadet
segments.text: Sir, new cadet Doe reports to the cadet--

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RED SASH #1: Is your last name Doe?

segments.speaker: Cadet
segments.text: No, sir.

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RED SASH #1: Then say your name, new cadet.

segments.speaker: Cadet
segments.text: Yes, sir.

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: "Is your last name Doe?" the red sash screams. "No, sir," says the new cadet. "Then say your name, new cadet," says the red sash. Words count, even footwork counts. New cadet Clinker, a jittery 18-year-old female cadet, finds this out when she steps a little too far forward.

segments.speaker: Cadet Clinker
segments.text: Sir, new cadet Clinker.

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RED SASH #1: New cadet, look where you're standing. I told you to step up to my line. You better learn how to follow orders, new cadet. New cadet--

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: The red sash asks her to do it again. This time, she stands in the right place, but she's forgotten what to say.

segments.speaker: Cadet Clinker
segments.text: Sir, new cadet Clinker reports to the--

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RED SASH #2: I tell you to drop it back, you drop it back--

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RED SASH #1: Are you showing emotion? Did I just see a smile come across your face, new cadet?

segments.speaker: Cadet Clinker
segments.text: No, sir.

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: (SUBJECT) RED SASH #1: You are like a rock. Maintain your military discipline at all times. You understand, new cadet?

segments.speaker: Cadet Clinker
segments.text: Yes, sir.

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: For these specially selected red sashes, breaking in the new cadets is a great honor. The day before, they've even practiced being hard on local civilians in a full rehearsal. Every year, a bunch of teachers, sons, daughters, groundskeepers from around town sign up for a fun day as practice cadets. Every year, a handful leave in tears.

segments.speaker: Cadet Mcleod
segments.text: Sir, new cadet McLeod reporting to the cadet in the-- in the red sash for the first time as ordered.

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: Drop your salute.

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: New cadet McLeod stutters on his first attempt. He's asked to drop his salute and start over. On this one day, almost 1,200 young men and women will make their report. If everyone did it right the first time, it would take about an hour. I don't see anyone go through the first time. It takes all day. New cadet McLeod tries again, but the words won't come.

segments.speaker: Cadet Mcleod
segments.text: Sir, n-new cadet McLeod-- new--

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: Drop your salute. [INTERPOSING VOICES]

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: Drop your salute, the red sash tells him. Are you a n-new cadet or a new cadet? New cadet, he says, forgetting the sir.

segments.speaker: Cadet Mcleod
segments.text: New cadet.

segments.speaker: Red Sash
segments.text: New cadet, are you going to put a 'sir' on that?

segments.speaker: Cadet Mcleod
segments.text: Yes, sir.

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: Poor new cadet McLeod has already screwed up twice. To get here, he spent 18 years excelling in nearly every way he can-- in schoolwork, in athletics, at student council meetings. He's beaten his way to the top of the 50,000 applicants who fill out requests for information forms.

segments.speaker: David Lipsky
segments.text: He's been interviewed by senators, congressmen. And now, here he is, in the last place he ever thought he'd find himself, a sudden death play audition. He only has to say one line. He draws a breath, tries one more time. And after letting go of his family, his hair, his clothes, he drops the last vestige of his civilian life-- he forgets his own name.

segments.speaker: Cadet Mcleod
segments.text: Sir, new cadet--

segments.speaker: Cadet Mcleod
segments.text: [INTERPOSING VOICES]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Lipsky-- his book following one cadet class at West Point for four years is called Absolutely American.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (HOST) IRA GLASS: Act 20-- The Greatest Moment I Ever Saw On a Stage. I'll say, first of all, that this moment that I saw caught me completely off guard. I was at a play where I was not expecting anything special. It was put on by an organization that works with teenagers. Storycatchers Theatre is what it's called.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And among other things, they get kids who are locked up in Chicago's juvenile detention center, The Audy Home, to write and perform musicals about their lives. This one was performed by teenage girls. OK, so we're in the detention center. Folding chairs have been set up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The girls' parents-- it's mostly mothers and grandmothers, very few men-- are sitting directly in front of the stage. And imagine for a minute what it's like to be one of those parents, OK? Your kid's locked up, possibly on very serious charges, some of these girls were. You're worried about what's going to happen to them next. You're probably still mad that they didn't listen to you in the first place and got into all this trouble and ended up behind bars.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What can theater possibly do for you in this situation? It seems like such an old-fashioned idea that it can do anything. So there's this one scene in the play.

segments.speaker: Actress 1
segments.text: Where'd you get these clothes from?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it's the story of this girl named Candace. And Candace basically wanted better clothes so the other kids at school wouldn't laugh at her. She steal some clothes from Nike Town. And she gets in trouble, she gets caught. And then she joins a gang to earn some money and be more popular.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Her mom finds some drugs in the house, and a gun, and feels completely betrayed because that was not how she raised her daughter. And one thing leads to another, and Candace gets locked up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then, the girl narrating the story says, and this is how Candace feels about her mom now. And then all the girls in the play come out on the stage and stand in a line, facing their mothers and grandmothers who are right there in front of them.

segments.speaker: Singers
segments.text: (SINGING) Mama, I'm sorry for what I have done. I was arrested and ended up here in the Audy Home. Oh, I'm sorry for putting you through all of this.

segments.speaker: Singers
segments.text: I know you are mad about the good times that we missed. I'm ready to come back home. I'm willing to make a change.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of the verses goes, "Mama, I'm sorry for making you come to court, for almost losing your job to give me moral support. Mama, I'm sorry for putting your through all this stress, for making you worry yourself and depressed. I'm ready to come back home. I'm willing to make a change."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And, by this time, the girls are all crying, the parents are all crying. And each girl has a cut-out little heart, like on Valentine's Day, like that, made from red construction paper, the size of your palm. And written on each one is the words, "I'm sorry."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And each girl goes out into the audience to where her mom is sitting, or her grandma is sitting, and hands her the heart. And the parents are crying, and the kids are crying, and everybody is hugging. It was really something.

segments.speaker: Singers
segments.text: (SINGING) --make a change. I'll do anything for you, mom. Please forget about yesterday. Mama, I'm sorry. [SNIFFLES]

segments.speaker: Singers
segments.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Mama, I'm sorry.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Here they were-- not just saying this to their mothers, but saying it publicly in front of the world, in front of their friends. Saying this thing that could be so hard to say in any case. Singing it out and hoping that it can heal something that is going to be hard to heal, no matter what you do.

segments.speaker: Singers
segments.text: (SINGING) Mama, I'm sorry. [SNIFFLES] I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Mama, I'm sorry.
